articles.title_zh: Stocks jump as oil prices tumble before midterms, tech shares rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as senior U.S. and Iranian officials signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 6.4% to $106.20 a barrel as of 9:50 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined 6.5% to $97.35 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of state said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to the state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency .
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term.
"Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.
"Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added.
—CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
Deals with six Green council groups that have condemned the motion are to remain in place, says Labour
UK politics live – latest updates
Labour is to stop cooperating with the Green party in 11 councils across England following an ultimatum for Greens in local government to disown a new policy stating that “Zionism is racism”.
A statement from Labour said coalitions or other deals with Greens would stop in all local authorities where they had refused to condemn the policy motion passed at their party conference last month, which also called for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.
Cooperation would cease on Arun, Derbyshire Dales, Havant, Lewes, Sheffield, Stafford, Warwick, Wealden, West Devon and West Suffolk councils, Labour said, and had already stopped in Runnymede because of the motion.
According to Labour, six Green council groups have condemned the motion, meaning deals will remain in place in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire, West Sussex. The same, it said, had happened with the West of England mayoralty, where the mayor is from Labour and the deputy mayor is a Green.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said the party had been clear that the motion, which has been met with unease by some Greens and has faced significant outside condemnation , “crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government”.
The Greens said they were “hugely disappointed” at the move, saying it would result in worse outcomes for residents in affected areas.
Phillipson said just over a fortnight ago that any Labour groups working with Green party politicians should review their agreements and end them unless they reject the motion, which Andy Burnham called “antisemitic” .
Some Greens, including the party’s former co-leader Adrian Ramsay, had called on local parties to renounce the policy, a stance that put him at odds with Zack Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales. The party’s official response was that the Greens would “not take lectures” from a Labour government that supplies arms to Israel.
The policy equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission has written to the Greens to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”.
Phillipson said: “Any local power-sharing arrangement cannot come at the expense of upholding the moral obligation we have to stand up for everyone in our communities and the values we share.
“We are pleased that some local Green parties have rightly opted to disavow this policy and have called on their party’s leadership to do the same. It is disappointing that some local Green parties have not met the conditions Labour has set out. Labour continues to oppose this divisive policy and calls on the Green party to do the right thing and rescind it.”
after newsletter promotion
She added: “The Labour party fought hard to root out antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics.”
In a joint statement, the Greens and the Local Government Association Green group said they were “hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents”.
They added: “Across the country, Green, Labour, independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change. Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.
“Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power-sharing agreements have often ignored the judgments of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.”
Under the party’s direct democracy rules, policy is decided by party members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, equating to approximately 0.4% of the total membership. It has been criticised by four of the Greens’ five MPs, as well as the former MP and party leader Caroline Lucas.
On Sunday, Ramsay said the Greens must fix their internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.

articles.title_orig: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
Chains in at least seven countries say fridge temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in dozens of their stores soared overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of losses in France.
Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg , the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been victims of a cyberattack.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of the cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in the wake of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
An ICA store at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed.”
The head of the national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around Sweden. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.
It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a store north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected stores, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”
He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their stores respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 stores.
“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons store to rise suddenly.
Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.
after newsletter promotion
In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said stores operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local stores had been affected.
At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.
Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 stores ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.
Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.
“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.
Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had knownand as yet unfixed flaws, he said.
“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he said. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”
In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.
The stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.
The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

articles.title_orig: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants
articles.title_zh: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants
articles.content_orig:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is due to announce her final decision on changes to immigration rules later - you'll be able to watch live above
This will include setting out reforms on the length of time people will have to be in the UK before becoming eligible for permanent settlement
Mahmood previously proposed extending the wait from the current five years to 10, in response to a period of high net migration, but has faced opposition from within her own party for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK
The Conservatives have said that any watering down of the proposal would be a "slap in the face to British taxpayers"
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) , also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible
Edited by Kieran Kelly and Manish Pandey
Chris Mason Political editor
At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago â and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.
"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.
The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.
Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.
But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend.
You can read Chris Mason's full analysis here.
The most recent immigration figures showed net migration was at its lowest level since 2012, excluding the Covid pandemic.
Data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in May showed that migration added 171,000 people to the UK's population last year, almost half the number seen in 2024.
The data also revealed that 93,525 people claimed asylum in the UK in the year to March 2026 - down 12% on the year prior, but still more than double that seen just before the pandemic.
The ONS said net migration continued to fall to levels last seen in early 2021 - when a new immigration system was introduced and Covid travel restrictions were in place.
Policy changes from early 2024 under the former Conservative government are likely to have made an impact on the net migration figures, including most overseas students being restricted from bringing family members to the UK.
The Labour government has retained the measures and in some cases expanded on them, including by introducing plans to end the recruitment of overseas care workers.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says it's "difficult to say" whether legal migration is too high or low in a recorded interview aired ahead of the home secretary's Commons address.
Speaking to ITV, Burnham said legal migration had "come right down" after official data released in May showed net migration had dropped to 171,000 in 2025, nearly half that of the previous year.
"I think when you have planned migration it's difficult to say whether it's too high or too
low because it's got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy, because if you
just put a number on it we may have a shortage in a certain area," he said.
However, he said migration overall was in a "much better place" as small boat crossing were also down, with 22,128 arrivals so far this year up to 31 October, down 40% from the same period last year.
"What I have argued is that migration and illegal migration changed significantly with Brexit and I think weâve got to be honest about that," he said.
Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" before she rejoined Cabinet
Mahmood has faced opposition from within the Labour Party over proposals to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
Before she re-joined the cabinet, Angela Rayner, who is now housing secretary, described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.
Trade unions had also put pressure on the government to soften its proposed changes, with delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backing a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in late September the reforms would need to "strike the right balance".
"But it just reflects that there's a consultation, there's different not just opinions from politicians, but obviously there's a range of views that have gone into that consultation, so we're in the process now of looking at that," he told LBC at the time.
In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."
This afternoon's Commons statement comes weeks after the home secretary signalled she was willing to rethink her plans at Labour's conference in Liverpool in September.
Mahmood acknowledged "some have said elements of these reforms are not fair" after mounting pressure from within the party.
She told delegates the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".
"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," she said.
"That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country."
'Indefinite leave to remain' refers to immigration status.
If you have indefinite leave to remain (ILR), it means there is no time limit on your ability to stay in the UK, and you are able to take up employment, self-employment or study.
People with ILR are also able to access public funds such as welfare benefits.
ILR approximates the concept of permanent residency in other countries, though that term has a different meaning under EU law.
It can lapse if you are outside the UK for a continuous period of two or more years.
ILR is different to the 'right of abode' which is automatically held by all British citizens, valid for life, and does not lapse if you live outside the UK.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants in the House of Commons this afternoon.
She had previously proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10, with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait.
The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government, known as the "Boriswave".
The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care after Mahmood faced opposition from within the government.
But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates and analysis.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Tech stocks aren't getting shredded for any old reason. It's actually very fundamental: Free cash flow is drying up for Big Tech leaders, and capex is rising dramatically.
Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack, given more realistic growth projections for AI.
The combined capex of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft rose by $36.9 billion in the third quarter to $201.9 billion, the team at The Kobeissi Letter calculated (chart below). This figure has more than doubled over the past 12 months, and is up a staggering 356% since the first quarter of 2024.
Big Tech has now spent $1.6 trillion on capex over the last three years, the strategists say. At the same time, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell $33.1 billion last quarter to a negative $26.4 billion, its lowest on record. Free cash flow among these tech beasts has fallen by $88.2 billion over the last year. Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the strategists estimate these four companies plan to spend another $232 billion on capex in the fourth quarter.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warned Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
In "MALE ANT PULLS OFF OWN WING TO MATE WITH QUEEN," three minutes of raw carnality from the BBC Earth's YouTube channel, a fat, ponderous male driver ant unsheathes spikes in his abdomen to lop off his right wing, and then lets dozens of much smaller female ants squeeze him into the queen's muddy bedchamber. It's possible that some of San Francisco's famously overworked and undersexed AI researchers have studied this footage for tutelage. That is where comparisons between ants and artificial intelligence would seem to begin and end. But then there is Anthropic.
Last week, the company submitted a financial prospectus for what may be the largest initial public offering ever , and announced it would list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Anthropic employees also call each other Ants — "a nickname that captures the collaborative, ego-light culture of the team," it notes in its government filing .
ANT is marching onto a busy little hill of creepy-crawly capitalism. It's at least the sixth insect-themed ticker in stock market history, joining a squishy cohort that includes FLY, BEE, BUG, HIVE, and GRUB — each of which have fared far better in the wild than on Wall Street. In 2014, The Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba launched The Ant Group, a giant fin-tech player. "Small is beautiful, small is powerful," Ant Group founder Jack Ma said of the name.
Are there risks in associating a company built on code with a bug? We've heard from the economists. What about the entomologists?
"It's not very affirming," says Deborah Gordon, an ecologist in Stanford's biology department who has studied ant behavior for more than 40 years. Her book "Ants at Work" begins, "The basic mystery about ant colonies is that there is no management." Calling employees Ants "is not only saying there's no central control, but also that they don't even know what they're doing," she said on a video call, while a large printed photo of a carpenter ant lurked in her background. She also noted that all worker ants are female. "That's probably not true of the engineers at Anthropic ."
Andrew Suarez, an ant ecologist at the University of Illinois, was relieved that the ant story of the week wasn't "How do I kill them in my house?" and had some advice for the new breed of Ants. In ant societies, cheating "is a very good strategy when it's rare," and a terrible one once everybody does it, which is worth knowing for anyone deploying fleets of AI agents , he told me over video, while a mammoth trap-jaw ant from a poster for the sci-fi horror movie "Empire of the Ants" glowered behind him. Suarez added that some colonies settle border disputes without bloodshed: Workers size each other up and "stand on their little toes like stilts," and the side that looks outmatched withdraws. Perhaps debates among AI safety researchers could be settled on stilettos.
Rob Dunn, a professor of applied ecology at North Carolina State University, observed that a leafcutter colony can hold a million workers in underground chambers that "might read as small office cubicles," he said. "No worker would have a perspective on what's happening in a different cubicle. They just do their part." The queen serves namely to make eggs. "I don't know what the Anthropic analogy is," he added. "Maybe that's tokens ."
Some entomologists worry about how Ants may threaten ants. What will data centers' thirst for water mean for the red harvester ants in drought-stricken Arizona that Gordon has spent dozens of summers studying? What will their constant hum mean for insects that communicate through vibration? Others are seeking guidance from ants, rather than their bosses, on how to better use AI. Next week, Dunn is convening a meeting of entomologists to discuss what lessons scout bees and ants "might offer for thinking about AI models and AI agents."
Dunn began his career in the Amazon rainforest; now, he notes, if you search for "Amazon" you get page after page of results for the company. "Every biologist will have a sad day when they go looking for an actual ant and instead find an Anthropic employee ," he says. Paul Rudd (Ant-Man), Woody Allen (the lead in 1998's "Antz"), NBA star Anthony "Ant" Edwards, and the nu-metal band Alien Ant Farm may also be sad. "The deeper sadness is how few people are paying attention to the world outside the digital world."
In the insectarium at the American Museum of Natural History one late afternoon last week, thousands of leafcutter ants were doing thousands of things: slinking, circling, bonking into one another, falling upside down, drowning, crawling, pausing, tickling, sawing, huddling. Nearby, a mother sang "The Ants Go Marching" to her toddler. "Holy shit," said a young man watching an ant carry a leaf chunk 10 times the size of its body over its head while scaling a pole. Dunn had told me what to look for: individuals "doing absolutely the wrong thing," and scurrying yonder. That wiggle is how a colony finds a new leaf, a new path, a new tree, he said. "That little wiggle is really important."
Anthropic burst into public consciousness with an extraordinarily rapid gestation more common in the natural world than in capitalism. Founded just five years ago, it now stands on the brink of becoming one of the most valuable companies in the world. Many people who had never heard of it until recently now debate whether it will be responsible for the destruction of the planet.
Yet the real ants have achieved a scale that any tech company would envy. There are some 20 quadrillion ants in the world. If Anthropic had a dollar for every ant, the Ants would have to expand its expected $2 trillion IPO by 10,000. Ants have existed for 150 million years. "They will be around long after we're all gone," said Dunn.
Most ants have never been studied, Dunn said. A graduate student of his, who had gone out looking for ants after a breakup, photographed a vampire ant near Raleigh that had been seen only once before. It hasn't been seen since. "Even as we feel so fancy," Dunn said, the world is "fundamentally undiscovered." Also, he added as we were hanging up, ants are delicious.

articles.title_orig: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.title_zh: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology on Monday said it will buy optical components maker Lumentum to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
"AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," said Marvell Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy in a release. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come."
Since the tie-up is a fixed ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
Marvell shares slumped 3%, while Lumentum's stock declined about 4% before the bell.

Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.
IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
"If they choose honest diplomacy, we are ready to engage," IRNA quoted Araghchi as saying. "If they intend to deceive us and launch military operations, they will face a response more bitter and forceful than before."
The Iranian Navy claimed Monday that another oil tanker had caught on fire after striking a sea mine near the eastern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, which is closely linked with Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The report cited the Navy as saying the unnamed vessel had struck a mine while attempting to use shipping lanes through the strait that Iran considers unauthorized and unsafe, but which the Trump administration and U.S. military have repeatedly claimed are free and open.
The tanker had switched off its navigation systems, Fars said, referring to a common practice by commercial vessels trying to obscure their movements in the region.
Tanker owners should take a lesson from the fate of vessels that violate Iran's rules by trying to transit the strait without authorization from Tehran, the report cited the navy as saying.
On Friday, despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that the southern shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe to navigate, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in the month of October alone, a record high.
The Iranian regime said earlier Monday that 11 ships had "caught fire" in or near the Strait of Hormuz in the last nine days alone.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran had presented Qatari mediators with a proposal to shorten the implementation period of a potential deal with the U.S. to just two days from seven.
In an interview with Al Jazeera , Araghchi said: "The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days."
The Iranian minister added, however, that Tehran's conditions for a deal to end the war remain the same.
The Islamic Republic regime has demanded that the U.S. release frozen Iranian financial assets, lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as sanctions, and cease hostilities on all fronts, including Israel's battle with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. In exchange, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping traffic and commit to further talks on its nuclear program.
Under the original seven-day implementation proposed by Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz would have been reopened on the sixth day.
With the shortened implementation period, according to a statement on the Iranian government website, "a series of measures will be taken by the United States on the first day, and on the second day, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and maritime traffic will return to its previous conditions."
Iran's government-run broadcaster IRIB said Monday that 11 oil tankers had "caught fire" in the Strait of Hormuz in the previous nine days, disputing U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper's assertion last week that "all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
In a post on X, IRIB said the 11 tankers had caught on fire since Oct. 25, the day on which it claimed Cooper made his recent fly-over of the strait.
The Iranian network offered no evidence, but claimed some of the vessels sank "to the depths of the sea."
Since the start of the war in February, Iran has targeted vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to assert control over the narrow waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's crude oil supply typically passed prior to the conflict.
Cooper said last week in a Friday video statement that he saw no Iranian navy vessels in the strait during his flyover earlier in the week.
Later Friday, however, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the month of October alone, a record high.
The U.S. military and President Trump have repeatedly declared Iran's navy destroyed and insisted that southern shipping lanes through the strait are available to merchant vessels, but ongoing Iranian threats and attacks have kept the risks and costs for shippers high, which has helped Tehran keep maintain pressure on global energy prices.
Iranian officials repeated warnings Monday of possible gas shortages for residents ahead of the winter, and they called on people to conserve the resource.
First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said he had to be honest about the stability of Iran's gas network in the colder months, as he asked the public to help conserve it.
Aref cited "imbalances accumulated over previous years and war-related damages," and warned that prices would increase for consumers who fail to conserve.
It is not the first time an Iranian official has warned about shortages. On October 25 , Iran's parliament speaker said natural gas consumption across Iran had to be reduced by 10%.
Iran's economy has been devastated by years of international sanctions, and the U.S. turn to economic warfare after the initial bombing campaigns of the ongoing conflict have strained finances for Tehran even further. The regime has not shown any willingness to bend on its demands to end the war, however, despite the economic pain for most Iranians.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.
Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.
President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.

articles.title_zh: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance detailed that the resulting net outflows represent just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets under management.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
On Monday, the exchange said it has covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount. The outstanding 5% consists of smaller tokens outside of the top 10 cryptocurrencies, whose assets are less liquid and will take longer to source.
Here's what you need to know:
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Over the weekend, the FBI said the attack was linked to North Korea.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Customer withdrawals were temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses.
Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches.
"This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
Around $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, according to Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder at blockchain analytics company Elliptic.
The attack has rattled crypto markets, and bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) traded at around $77,700 on Monday. Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.

articles.title_orig: Where things stand on Iran after tense weekend as its delegation has left Qatar
articles.title_zh: Where things stand on Iran after tense weekend as its delegation has left Qatar
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s military is warning that if all-out war breaks out again with the United States and Israel, it will be longer and more costly than their rivals expect.
Iran’s armed forces could deploy new weapons and tactics against the US, Israel and other countries, which would be the third major conflict between the countries since June last year.
There have been increasing signs that the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began on February 28, could restart after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the war with Iran will end “very soon one way or the other” and Tehran should agree a deal or “the hammer” will come down.
Hossein Kanani Moghaddam, a former senior IRGC commander, told Al Jazeera that despite extensive blows to the Iranian armed forces during US and Israeli strikes earlier this year, they are now in better operational shape compared with previous conflicts.
“In terms of offence, our target database has significantly expanded, the range, accuracy and warheads of our missiles have improved and our drone capabilities have increased,” he said.
New enemy assets were being identified and operations in additional geographical areas were being planned, he added. Arkaminia said that previously undisclosed capabilities and targets would be revealed – and used – if Iran is attacked again.
Commanders from Iran’s General Staff of Armed Forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Islamic Republic of Iran Army are reported to have recently met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss what steps will be taken if attacked again. The response will be immediate and could go beyond the West Asia region , they said.
The IRGC was “100 percent ready” to confront another attack, spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Sunday evening, describing “maximum deterrence” as a goal Iran would reach in the near future.
Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the commanders would rely on “asymmetric warfare” tactics that would compensate for the superiority of US military equipment.
He added that “some weaponry was renovated and new equipment was added along with new tactics” during the brief ceasefire period that came after the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US.
Last month, state television showed an underground drone production line. The authorities also showcased an upgraded version of the Arash attack drone and claimed that its warhead had doubled to 100kg with improved guidance.
According to a Reuters investigation published last week, numerous military agencies linked with Iran’s defence establishment have evaded sanctions and funnelled billions into military imports to replenish the IRGC. The imports between January 2025 and June this year from China, Russia and Germany to fuel missile and drone production included rocket propellants, explosives, detonators, titanium and heavy-duty trucks that could be used as launchers.
Many Iranian missile defence systems, radars and other equipment were hit during the war. But Kanani Moghaddam said remaining and newly developed systems were becoming more accurate, pointing to the targeting of a US-built F-35 and other warplanes and drones as successes that can be replicated and expanded upon.
“At sea, we have shown that we can easily target supertankers,” he said regarding transit through the Strait of Hormuz that is deemed “unauthorised” by Iranian authorities. He said Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels in September prompted them to stop venturing into the critical waterway since. But the US has continued its naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, while Iran’s civilian population and infrastructure remain largely exposed if the war resumes.
Tehran and other cities across the country lack shelters or early warning systems to protect civilians. Authorities have not reported any progress regarding the promised shelters and gaps in public warning arrangements.
Iran’s electricity grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, petrochemical and steel manufacturers and roads and railways could also be attacked again, making life even more difficult amid the economic crisis.
During both wars, many senior political and military figures of the Islamic Republic were killed by US and Israeli strikes.
The new supreme leader has not been seen or heard from since replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in early March, ostensibly for security reasons.
This has led to tighter domestic security controls, and prompted some voices from within the establishment to raise concerns and demand accountability for intelligence failures and protection of leadership.
“We have been hit and hit hard,” state-linked analyst Hamzeh Rahim Safavi said during a televised debate on Saturday. “The main cause is intelligence weakness, but no one talks about it or is held accountable”.
The analyst is the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander-in-chief of the IRGC who currently serves as a senior military adviser to the supreme leader. The analyst said calls by hardliners to acquire a nuclear bomb would not repair intelligence and security weaknesses.
But Esmaeil Kowsari, a former IRGC division commander now a parliamentary national-security commission member, told local media last week that even though the supreme leader and others were assassinated, “the enemies did not reach their main goals”. He said the goals were to overthrow the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran.
“On the eve of their elections, the Americans are trying to pretend that they have achieved victory by causing a ruckus and launching psychological operations, but that is not the truth,” Kowsari said.

articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title_zh: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
articles.content_orig:
Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe.
Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically.
The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems.
“We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.
The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked.
SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores.
The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel.
Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman’s CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain.
Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month.
The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.
One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France.
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email.
Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.
There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France.
However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war.
European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.
European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said the attacks were “a deliberate attempt ⁠to disrupt” EU food supplies and undermine public ‌confidence.
“These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.
A spokesperson for The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium told Al Jazeera that the rising number of cyberattack incidents, especially those resulting from the targeted use of AI, is an evolving trend.
However, they added, “we may never be able to identify … who is behind this attack”.

articles.title_orig: Audemars Piguet Introduces Three Supersonnerie Watches And Two Stone-Dial Code 11.59 Models
articles.title_zh: Audemars Piguet Introduces Three Supersonnerie Watches And Two Stone-Dial Code 11.59 Models
articles.content_orig:
Audemars Piguet expands its Royal Oak and Code 11.59 collections with five new references that explore two very different aspects of the manufacture’s watchmaking. Three new Minute Repeater Supersonnerie models showcase its work in acoustic engineering, while two 38mm Code 11.59 Selfwinding watches introduce natural stone dials in gold obsidian and black onyx. The releases range from technically complex chiming watches to more restrained time-only models, with each offering a different interpretation of the collections’ long-standing designs.
The three minute repeaters share the same hand-wound caliber 2953 and Supersonnerie technology. Two arrive in the 42mm Royal Oak line, including the first pink gold version of this execution, while the third is a new iteration of the 41mm Code 11.59 Minute Repeater Supersonnerie. The two stone-dial watches, meanwhile, offer a more compact take on the Code 11.59, with cases in yellow or pink gold.
Audemars Piguet introduced its Supersonnerie technology in 2016 with the Royal Oak Concept RD#1. The result of eight years of development, the project brought together watchmakers, musicians, and researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL). The objective was to improve the acoustic performance of a wristwatch minute repeater, a complication that presents particular challenges when producing a clear chime from a mechanism housed inside a relatively small case.
The patented construction uses gongs mounted on a dedicated soundboard. Combined with an innovative case construction and a newly developed regulator, this approach improves the striking mechanism’s acoustic performance. The latest watches use caliber 2953, a manually wound 30 × 6mm movement. It comprises 362 components and 32 jewels, operates at 3 Hz, and offers a minimum guaranteed power reserve of 72 hours. In addition to the minute repeater, the movement drives the hours, minutes, and small seconds.
The first of the new Royal Oak references, 26591TI.OO.1252TI.08 , features a 42mm titanium case and an integrated bracelet in the same material. Its green dial has a satin-finished sunburst motif and a smoked effect that darkens towards the edge. A matching green small-seconds counter maintains the color scheme, while 18K white gold Royal Oak hands and silver-toned 18K pink gold hour markers provide contrast. The indexes and central hands are filled with luminescent material.
As with other Royal Oak models, the case combines satin-brushed and polished surfaces. These alternating finishes create depth and detail across the watch’s angular architecture. The titanium reference measures 14 mm thick and is water-resistant to 20 meters.
The second Royal Oak Minute Repeater Supersonnerie, reference 26591OR.OO.1252OR.01 , offers a warmer interpretation. For the first time, Audemars Piguet presents this model in 18K pink gold, pairing the metal with a lovely brown Grande Tapisserie dial. The small-seconds counter follows the dial’s color, while the hands and lume-filled hour markers are also pink gold. A matching integrated bracelet completes the design. This watch shares the exact case dimensions and water resistance of its titanium counterpart.
The third watch brings Supersonnerie technology to the Code 11.59 collection. This 41mm reference 26395BC.OO.D009CR.01 is a new iteration of 2023’s Minute Repeater Supersonnerie. Its 18K white gold case features a fully polished middle, while the smoked sapphire dial reveals AP’s caliber 2953 beneath. The minute track and the rim around the small-seconds counter use galvanic growth to create additional texture and depth.
White gold baton hands and hour markers complete the display. The watch comes on a gray alligator strap with an 18K white gold folding clasp. With a 13.6mm profile, it is slightly slimmer than the two Royal Oak references, though it shares their 20m water resistance. All three watches have a price on request .
Alongside the minute repeaters, Audemars Piguet introduces two 38mm Code 11.59 Selfwinding models with natural stone dials. One uses gold obsidian, while the other features black onyx. Each material brings a different surface and character to the collection, with the finishing process intended to reveal the stone’s particular color, texture, and depth.
The yellow gold reference 77410BA.OO.A604CR.01 features a natural obsidian dial with a sunburst motif. Gold obsidian contains mineral inclusions that produce reflective details within its dark surface. The finish brings these variations into view, creating subtle changes as light moves across the dial. Yellow gold hands filled with luminescent material and gold-toned hour markers complement the case. A shimmering brown inner bezel and black alligator strap add further contrast.
The second model, reference 77410OR.OO.A001CR.01, combines an 18K pink gold case with a mirror-polished black onyx dial. The stone’s deep black surface provides a backdrop for baguette-cut diamond indexes, totaling 0.37 carats. Pink gold hands filled with luminescent material tie the dial to the case, while a black inner bezel and a shiny black alligator strap maintain the darker aesthetic.
Both watches measure 38 mm across and 9.6 mm thick. They feature double-curved, glare-proofed sapphire crystals on the front and back and offer water resistance to 30 meters. The yellow gold version retails for CHF 45,500 , while the pink gold one costs CHF 54,100 .
Inside, the automatic caliber 5909 provides hours, minutes, and a central seconds hand. This 26.2 × 3.9mm movement consists of 174 components, including 29 jewels, and runs at 4 Hz. Its minimum guaranteed power reserve is 60 hours.
These five additions highlight two notably different areas of Audemars Piguet’s watchmaking. The Supersonnerie references emphasize the engineering behind a complex chiming complication, presenting the same movement across two dissimilar collection designs and three material executions. The two smaller Code 11.59 models, meanwhile, use natural stone to create distinct dial designs within a time-only format. Together, the releases expand the Royal Oak and Code 11.59 collections through different approaches to materials, finishing, and mechanical watchmaking.

articles.content_orig:
TheCoolist is a mood board for your headspace.
It sits next to every toilet, usually in a closed holder, and a Finnish cleaning expert says many people keep it far too long. In Scandinavia and Central Europe, home sites report that many households are now swapping the classic bristle toilet brush for a different design. Here’s what is replacing it, why cleaning pros say it’s more hygienic, and what it still can’t do.
According to the Norwegian site Dagens.no , many people are choosing a silicone brush over the traditional plastic one. The reasons it gives: there are no dense bristles for dirt to collect in, so the head rinses clean; the flexible head reaches the edges and hard-to-access areas; it tends to spray less; and it is often sold with a ventilated or wall-mounted holder that lets it dry faster. The site quotes Finnish cleaning expert Mari Breilin, who says plastic brushes should be replaced considerably more often than many people do. The price, it adds, is about the same as many ordinary brushes.
The British testing site Expert Reviews sums it up: bristles are “so tightly packed together that it’s impossible to clean them perfectly,” so “bacteria build-up on the brush is inevitable,” and they “need replacing much more often.” Cleaning expert Isabella Flores, of Sparkly Maid San Diego, told Tom’s Guide that silicone is non-porous, so it doesn’t absorb bacteria and organic matter the way plastic bristles can. It also dries faster and tolerates harsher disinfection, including boiling.
Silicone or not, the routine is what keeps it hygienic. Tom’s Guide recommends:
Silicone is not a miracle. Expert Reviews notes that silicone brushes shaped like regular ones “usually have weak bristles that don’t do a great job on stubborn dirt,” and that flat, spatula-style heads handle grime better, though you have to get used to a different technique. And no brush, silicone or bristle, is built to dissolve the hard mineral ring at the waterline. And whatever you choose, a brush kept damp in a closed holder will still breed bacteria.
For that waterline ring, here’s the best way to remove limescale from the toilet . The bathroom is changing in other ways too, like the option replacing toilet paper , and the floor around the base deserves attention: see why people are spraying vinegar around the toilet .
A flat silicone head, an open holder and a date to replace it. That’s the trick.

articles.title_orig: Deportees Turn to Social Media to Share Life in Countries They Barely Know
articles.title_zh: Deportees Turn to Social Media to Share Life in Countries They Barely Know
articles.content_orig:
“We are living through the greatest transformation that we have seen in our lifetimes, and likely for a significant time before that,” two-time Surgeon General Vivek Murthy told an audience at New York City’s flagship public library on Oct. 28, comparing the advent of artificial intelligence to the advent of nuclear weaponry in terms of the need for carefully thought out safety standards. “We're at a branch point,” he added. “What should the future really look like, what are we trying to protect and preserve?”
Murthy was not alone in sounding the alarm. Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media , the organizer of the conference, told the mostly supportive crowd that recent history had proved that the industry leaders or, as he called them “tech broligarchs,” could not be relied upon to create digital information systems that were safe or healthy for children. “We did not get out in front of social media in time,” he told the gathering. “This is the moment. AI is a bigger deal. It's basically social media on steroids.”
New York’s governor Kathy Hochul seemed to underscore the point when she made an unscheduled stop at the daylong summit to announce new regulations around chatbots interactions with children. The bill was designed to ensure that AI agents do not impersonate humans or communicate in a way that suggests they have a relationship with a child. “It's happening so quickly,” said Hochul of the technological changes. “It's almost impossible for parents to know what's going on, for elected officials to stay ahead of it, and we certainly have learned the lesson that we can't count on the companies to put out products that are responsible and that put children first.”
Specifically, the new law, which goes into effect in January, will ban chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, secrecy, or isolation and from discouraging children to seek help from other humans. They will also be banned from engaging in sexually explicit interactions and restricted from using a child’s past personal or health information in later conversations.
For the attendees and speakers at the summit, who ranged from Chelsea Clinton and Columbia law professor Tim Wu (onstage) to Uma Thurman (in the audience), the announcement was a good start, although many bemoaned the lack of federal regulation, around both AI and social media. “To this day, 2026, our federal government and Congress has still—nearly a quarter century after the advent of social media—failed to announce anything to protect our kids,” said Murthy, who is now chair of the advisory board of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute , which studies, tests, and rates AI platforms for children.
Panelists called for a range of protective and preventative remedies for what they described as the coming tsunami of AI, including requiring more data transparency from tech companies by enabling regulatory agencies and researchers to get more access to the information they’re holding, using consumer-protection laws to ensure that AI models have been rigorously tested for potential negative outcomes, adopting the European model of not allowing AI companies to deploy their platforms until they have proved they are safe, or even instituting criminal penalties for AI companies who unleash unsafe technologies. “As a former prosecutor, I can tell you one thing,” said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who earlier this month won a $25 billion judgment against Meta. “When you bring out handcuffs, suddenly everything changes.”
Not all the issues around AI can be solved by the law, however. One concern is the socialization of very young children by AI, including via voice-activated assistants like Alexa or very agreeable AI-enabled toys. “What do kids start to learn to expect from social practice? Do they expect someone to always agree with them? Is it always easy? Is it always like a transaction?” asked Dana Suskind , an early-childhood expert and professor at the University of Chicago. Human relationships are a lot messier, she noted. “They're chaotic, and that sort of mess is where a lot of learning happens.” Parents, who were caught off-guard by the influence of social media and digital devices, need to be educated about AI and encouraged that their imperfect parenting, as well as other human interaction, is vastly more beneficial to children than an AI companion, she said.
The summit also touched on the enormous implications AI is having on education and students’ ability to work and learn, when answers are in such ready supply. “MIT just did a report saying every assignment at MIT could be done by generative AI,” said John King, a former U.S. Secretary of Education and current chancellor of State University in New York. King is considering major changes to student assessment. “We have to make sure we are seeing the students do the work, and we have to make sure they're getting those foundational skills,” he said. “It literally means every faculty member reassessing what they assign and how they measure student learning.” And, as Clinton pointed out, this is an equity issue too. “We know that in families with less than $30,000 of household income, teenagers are three times more likely to either largely or entirely do their homework through artificial intelligence than those households with family incomes of $75,000 or more,” she said.
At the same time, students need to be prepared to enter a workforce in which AI skills are not optional. For those who have mastered them, the future is very bright. “The people coming in learn much more rapidly because AI gives them more capacity than they've had before,” said Gene Sykes, chairman of global mergers and acquisitions at Goldman Sachs of the banking giant’s new recruits. “So somebody, within a month, can be doing incredibly productive work.” If good education in AI is distributed unevenly, some graduates will be vastly better prepared for a career than others, further exacerbating wealth inequities.
While there was little consensus on the immediate steps to take as AI arrives, there was no argument that it will be consequential for children, families, and generations to come. “As we go into this age of transformation,” Murthy noted, “the question forced upon us is the following: What aspects of human existence do we want to protect and preserve at all costs?”

articles.title_orig: Python struggles to escape as more than 10 mongooses bite and tug to defend one of their own
articles.title_zh: Python struggles to escape as more than 10 mongooses bite and tug to defend one of their own
articles.content_orig:
A python that appeared to grab a mongoose soon faced an unexpected barrage of more than 12 members of the small mammal's group fighting back.
The video , shared on Instagram by Bestial Nature (@bestialnature) starts with the attack underway. It appears that the python has one mongoose wrapped tightly in its grip, while at least a dozen furry friends and family members assault the snake from every angle.
A colony or pack can offer a mongoose protection. Members may confront a threat together when one of them is endangered. This form of defense occurs in some social species of these small, carnivorous mammals.
The snake eventually lunges at other mongooses, but the horde appears to be too much for the serpent to handle. The video ends before there is a conclusion, but the mongoose clan seems to be overwhelming the snake, so it's hard to imagine it ends well for the reptile.
Several details about the encounter remain unclear. The account does not identify either species, provide a location, or establish what ultimately happened to the animals.
Mammals, birds, and reptiles are usual python prey, with the mix depending on the snake's species and size. A mongoose is not a staple food, but pythons may take the opportunity to eat one, according to A-Z Animals.
A python applies pressure by coiling around an animal after first taking hold with its teeth. Pythons, unlike cobras, are nonvenomous. A python's species matters when considering its length. Some species grow to just a few feet long, while the largest can exceed 20 feet.
Forests, grasslands, rocky terrain, savannas, scrublands, and open woodlands all provide mongoose habitat, though species use them differently. These mammals occur mainly in Africa and Asia.
Pythons, meanwhile, live in forests, wetlands, rocky areas, grasslands, and scrublands, creating some overlap with mongoose habitats. The snakes' range covers Africa and Asia and extends to Australia and parts of Oceania.
Resistance to venom does not prevent a python from constricting a mongoose. According to A-Z Animals, some mongoose species resist particular neurotoxins, especially those in cobra venom. In encounters with snakes, mongooses also depend on agility and quick bites.
A venomous bite can still endanger a mongoose despite its resistance to certain venoms. According to A-Z Animals, that resistance in some mongooses comes from alterations to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that make them less susceptible to those toxins.

articles.title_orig: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.title_zh: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
